title: IPv4 Addressing
summary: Every device on the internet needs a unique logical address. Learn how IPv4 packs a 32-bit number into dotted decimal, how address classes and private ranges work, and what the subnet mask marks.

blocks.markdown:
An **IP address** (Internet Protocol address) is a unique **logical** label assigned to each device on a network so packets can find their destination across any number of routers.

- **Logical** means software-assigned, unlike MAC addresses which are burned into hardware.
- IPv4 uses **32-bit** addresses, giving ~4.3 billion unique values.
- Every packet carries a source and destination IP — routers read these to forward it hop by hop.

blocks.subTitle: 32 bits and dotted decimal
blocks.markdown:
An IPv4 address is **32 bits** written as four **octets** (8-bit groups) separated by dots — called **dotted-decimal** notation.

- Each octet ranges **0–255** (2⁸ = 256 values).
- Example: `192.168.1.10` → four octets: `192`, `168`, `1`, `10`.
- Computers store it as one 32-bit integer; the dots are only for human readability.

Every IPv4 address splits into two parts:

- **Network portion** — identifies which network the device belongs to. All devices on the same network share this prefix.
- **Host portion** — identifies the specific device within that network.

Example: in `192.168.1.10` with a 24-bit network portion, `192.168.1` is the network and `10` is the host. The **subnet mask** marks where the split happens — covered below.
Early IPv4 used **classful** addressing — the first bits of an address determined its class and the fixed network/host split.

blocks.subTitle: Class table
blocks.markdown:
The five classes at a glance.

| Class | Range | Use |
|---|---|---|
| A | 1–126.x.x.x | Large orgs (16M hosts) |
| B | 128–191.x.x.x | Mid orgs (65K hosts) |
| C | 192–223.x.x.x | Small nets (254 hosts) |
| D | 224–239.x.x.x | Multicast |
| E | 240–255.x.x.x | Reserved/research |

Classes D and E are not used for regular unicast devices. Today classless [subnetting-vlsm](subnetting-vlsm) has replaced rigid classes.

**Public IP addresses** are globally unique and routable on the internet — assigned by ISPs.

**Private IP addresses** (defined in **RFC 1918**) are reserved for internal networks and are **not routed** on the public internet. Any organization can reuse them freely inside their own network.

**RFC 1918** is the standard that reserves three private ranges — saving public address space.

blocks.subTitle: RFC 1918 private ranges
blocks.markdown:
The three private ranges you must know.

| Range | Class | Hosts |
|---|---|---|
| 10.0.0.0/8 | A | ~16 million |
| 172.16.0.0/12 | B | ~1 million |
| 192.168.0.0/16 | C | ~65 thousand |

Your home router hands out `192.168.x.x` addresses. NAT (Network Address Translation) maps private IPs to one public IP at the border.

Several IPv4 addresses have fixed, reserved meanings:

- **127.0.0.1** — **loopback** address. Traffic to this address never leaves the host; used to test the local network stack. The whole `127.x.x.x` block is reserved for loopback.
- **0.0.0.0** — means "this host" or "any address" depending on context (e.g. a server binding to all interfaces).
- **255.255.255.255** — **limited broadcast** — sent to every device on the local network segment.
- **x.x.x.255** — **directed broadcast** to all hosts in a subnet (often blocked by routers).

A **subnet mask** is a 32-bit value that marks which part of an IP address is the network and which is the host.

- Written in the same dotted-decimal form: e.g. `255.255.255.0`.
- Bits set to **1** → network portion. Bits set to **0** → host portion.
- Applied via a bitwise AND with the IP address to extract the network address.

Example: IP `192.168.1.10` AND mask `255.255.255.0` → network `192.168.1.0`. The full math of splitting networks lives in [subnetting-vlsm](subnetting-vlsm).

blocks.subTitle: CIDR notation
blocks.markdown:
**CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)** notation shortens the mask to a slash and a number — the count of network bits.

- `192.168.1.0/24` means the first **24 bits** are the network portion, the last 8 are hosts.
- `/24` equals mask `255.255.255.0`; `/8` equals `255.0.0.0`.
- CIDR replaced rigid classful addressing and enables efficient address allocation.

Common misconceptions:

- **"127.0.0.1 is the only loopback."** The whole `127.0.0.0/8` block is loopback — any address in it stays local.
- **"Private IPs are secure because they're hidden."** NAT obscures them, but internal traffic is not encrypted. Security needs firewalls and TLS.
- **"Class A, B, C still govern routing."** Classful addressing is obsolete — all modern routing is classless (CIDR). Routers use the mask, not the first octet class.

blocks.subTitle: How many bits in IPv4
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address, and how many unique addresses does that give?**

**32 bits** — 4 octets of 8 bits each. 2³² = **~4.3 billion** unique addresses. That sounds large but IPv4 exhaustion was declared in 2011, which is why private ranges + NAT extend the space and [ipv6](ipv6) was created.

blocks.subTitle: Public vs private IP
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a public and a private IP address?**

A **public IP** is globally unique and routable on the internet — assigned by your ISP. A **private IP** (RFC 1918 ranges: 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) is only valid inside a local network and cannot be routed on the internet. NAT translates private-to-public at the network border.

blocks.subTitle: Loopback and 0.0.0.0
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the loopback address, and what does 0.0.0.0 mean?**

`127.0.0.1` (the **loopback**) routes traffic back to the same host without hitting the network — used to test local services. `0.0.0.0` is a meta-address meaning *any/all interfaces* in a server bind context, or *this host* when an address is unknown (e.g. DHCP requests).

**Q: What does the subnet mask do?**

It marks the split between network and host bits. Bitwise AND with the IP yields the network address — routers use this to decide where to forward a packet.
